newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Waigel says sees no problems clarifying ERM2.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Waigel says sees no problems clarifying ERM2.

text.p: Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on Monday he saw no unsurmountable problems in clarifying details of a new exchange rate mechanism and a so-called stability pact left unresolved at a weekend meeting.

European Union finance ministers and central bank governors decided at a weekend meeting on the framework of a new European rate mechanism, known as ERM2, intended to group the currencies of countries unable to join monetary union in the first round.
They also agreed the basis of a stability pact to ensure that those countries which do join the single currency maintian fiscal discipline long-term.

But the stability pact in particular is far from being fully in place. Many of the precise details of the plan -- which will be crucial to its effectiveness -- were simply referred to working committees after the Dublin talks.

Waigel, who said on Saturday he was satisfied with the progress made this weekend, said today in response to a question at a political party meeting that he did not expect major problems in finding agreement on the outstanding points.
"With a bit of good will, I see no more insurmountable problems," Waigel said.

Details of the stability pact that remain to be worked out include how sanctions will be imposed for those countries that do not continue to keep their deficits in check after a single currency is launched in 1999, he said.
Participants must also narrow the definitions of terms such as "exceptional" and "temporary", defining the precise circumstances that would allow a country to acceptably exceed the criteria, he said.

Waigel initially proposed the concept of a stability pact as a means of ensuring that countries which pass the economic test set for entry to the single currency do not later become lax in their fiscal policies.

Over the weekend, officials said a German proposal calling for a deposit of 0.25 percent of GDP for each percentage point of excess deficit was still on the table alongside a European Commission proposal for a smaller deposit per percentage point, capped at a maximum of 0.5 percent.

On Britain's participation in European Monetary Union, Waigel said, "I hope that the currency union includes as many stability countries as possible. And the United Kingdom is one of these stability countries."
The financial world is greatly interested that Britain not exclude itself from European integration and EMU, he said.
